notes.meaning: Around May, during the dry wheat harvest, Samson went to visit his wife. He brought a young goat as a gift to make peace and asked to go into her room. Her father blocked the door and would not let him inside.

The father explained that he assumed Samson had completely abandoned and hated her, so he gave her to Samson's best man. He then offered her younger sister instead. Samson could not accept this offer, because God's law forbade marrying two living sisters, and the father's excuse was an insult.

Samson refused the father's offer and announced that he was fully justified in striking back. He felt blameless because the Philistines had wronged him first. He decided to use this personal insult as a reason to attack Israel's oppressors.

Samson went out and gathered three hundred jackals or foxes, which often roamed in packs in the hills. He tied them together in pairs by their tails and fastened a torch between each pair. Tying them tail-to-tail kept them from running straight into their dens.

He lit the torches and released the animals into the dry fields of the Philistines. The frightened animals ran through the countryside, setting fire to the harvested grain, the standing crops, and the valuable olive groves and vineyards. This ruined the food supply of the Philistines for the entire year.

When the Philistines found out Samson caused the fire because his father-in-law gave his wife away, they turned on the woman's family. A mob marched to their house and burned both the woman and her father to death. Tragically, she suffered the very death she had tried to avoid when she betrayed Samson earlier.

Samson warned the Philistines that their brutal act would not stop him from taking revenge. Even though they killed the family that had wronged him, their cruelty only increased his anger. He promised he would not rest until he paid them back in full.

Samson launched a fierce, crushing attack against the Philistines and killed many of them. After the fight, he retreated to the rocky cliff of Etam in Judah and stayed in a cave. There he was safe from an immediate counterattack.

A Philistine army marched up into the hill country of Judah to hunt down Samson. They set up camp and spread their soldiers out near a place later called Lehi. They intended to force the men of Judah to produce Samson.

The leaders of Judah asked the Philistines why they had marched into their territory with an army. The Philistines answered that their only goal was to capture Samson and punish him for burning their fields. They had no quarrel with the rest of Judah as long as Samson was surrendered.

Three thousand men of Judah went to the cave at Etam to find Samson. Instead of rallying behind him to fight for their freedom, they scolded him for upsetting their Philistine rulers. Samson answered simply that he had only given the Philistines what they deserved.

The men of Judah told Samson they had come to tie him up and hand him over to the Philistines. Samson agreed to surrender peacefully, but only if they swore not to kill him themselves. He loved his people and refused to fight his own countrymen.

The men of Judah promised they would not harm him, but would tie him tightly and surrender him to the enemy. They bound him with two strong, brand-new ropes and led him out of the rocky cave. Samson allowed himself to be bound, trusting God to deliver him.

As Samson arrived at Lehi, the Philistines shouted with joy, thinking their great enemy was helpless. At that moment, the Spirit of the Lord came mightily upon him. The strong ropes snapped off his arms and wrists as easily as burned flax threads falling apart in a fire.

Samson looked around and found the fresh, moist jawbone of a dead donkey that had not yet dried out and turned brittle. He picked it up and used it as a club, striking down one thousand Philistine soldiers. God gave him the strength to win a huge victory with a simple, crude tool.

Samson celebrated his victory with a short, clever poem. In Hebrew, the words for donkey and heap sound almost identical, creating a play on words. He sang that with the jawbone of a donkey, he had piled his enemies into heaps.

When Samson finished his song, he threw the jawbone away. He named the hill Ramath-lehi, which means Jawbone Hill or the Casting Away of the Jawbone. The name served as a lasting reminder of what took place there.

After the exhausting battle in the summer heat, Samson grew terribly thirsty and felt close to collapsing. He cried out to the Lord, openly admitting that God had won this great deliverance through him. He asked God not to let His servant die of thirst and fall into the hands of pagan enemies.

God answered Samson by splitting open a hollow basin in the ground at Lehi, and cool water flowed out. When Samson drank, his energy returned and he was fully refreshed. He named the spring En-hakkore, meaning the Spring of the One Who Called, and it remained there for generations.

Samson served as a leader and judge over Israel for twenty years during the period of Philistine oppression. Although he did not completely rid the land of the Philistines, he checked their power and defended God's people. His life showed that God can bring deliverance even in dark times.
